forces.title: Elevated geopolitical risks drive fertiliser price increases
forces.description: The US/Israel conflict with Iran, particularly impacting the Strait of Hormuz, has led to a sharp increase in European natural gas and crude oil prices. As natural gas is a key feedstock for nitrogenous fertilisers, and oil impacts transport/production, these higher energy costs are directly translating into a forecast 20% increase in fertiliser prices for 2026. This escalation poses significant cost pressure for fertiliser producers and downstream agricultural sectors.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: CBAM implemented for fertilisers to protect domestic industry
forces.description: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has come into effect, specifically applying to carbon-intensive imports like fertilisers. This policy aims to protect European producers from cheaper, higher-emission imports by levelling the playing field on carbon costs, encouraging green production, and addressing competitive disadvantages against regions with less stringent environmental regulations. This is a structural market intervention that can benefit European fertiliser manufacturers.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Long-term shift towards sustainable farming reduces fertiliser use
forces.description: There is a growing awareness among Irish farmers regarding the environmental benefits of using clover and multispecies swards to reduce reliance on traditional chemical fertilisers. While this transition is expected to take several years, it represents a structural shift in agricultural practices that will likely impact long-term fertiliser demand. This trend could act as a gradual headwind for conventional fertiliser producers.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Global food security concerns and potential government intervention
forces.description: Warnings from the World Bank highlight a threat to global food security due to fertiliser shortages and soaring agricultural costs, exacerbated by geopolitical conflicts. This situation may prompt government intervention to stabilize supply or manage prices, which could significantly alter market dynamics for the fertiliser industry. Such interventions could impose price controls or allocate supply, impacting manufacturers' operations and profitability.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Supply chain disruptions elevate feedstock and freight costs
forces.description: Geopolitical tensions, particularly those affecting the Middle East and shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz, are causing global supply chain disruptions. This leads to increased freight costs and limits the availability of critical raw materials, such as Sulfur, which is an input for phosphatic fertilisers. These disruptions add to operational complexities and cost pressures for fertiliser manufacturers, potentially impacting production continuity and margins.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Decreased cropland area to reduce fertiliser demand in Ireland
forces.description: The area devoted to tillage crops in Ireland is expected to decrease in 2026, leading to a likely reduction in fertiliser use on cropland. This trend reflects farmers' caution and responses to market conditions and weather, contributing to a slight contraction in a specific segment of fertiliser demand. This represents a headwind, albeit localized and potentially short-term, for fertiliser suppliers to the tillage sector.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Increased working capital needs for agricultural supply chain
forces.description: The rising input costs for agriculture, including fertilisers and fuel, are expected to increase working capital demand across the farming sector and its supply chain. This financial pressure on farmers may indirectly affect payment terms or order patterns for fertiliser suppliers, although Ireland shows some short-term resilience due to existing stock. Prolonged high costs could strain liquidity throughout the agricultural value chain.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Global farmer planting shifts impact fertiliser demand
forces.description: A prolonged escalation of the Middle East conflict could lead farmers globally to alter planting decisions, potentially favouring less energy-intensive crops that require less fertiliser, such as soya over maize. Such a shift in agricultural patterns would represent a long-term change in demand dynamics for various fertiliser types, creating a structural headwind for producers of high-intensity fertilisers if the trend becomes widespread.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Fertiliser prices to increase by 20% in Ireland due to geopolitical conflict
viewpoints.description: Teagasc forecasts that fertiliser prices in Ireland will be approximately 20% higher in 2026 compared to 2025. This increase is primarily driven by the sharp rise in European natural gas prices, which are heavily influenced by the US/Israel attacks on Iran. While a de-escalation of the conflict (as of early July 2026) might ease pressure, the structural link between energy costs and fertiliser production ensures sustained high prices, presenting a challenge for agricultural profitability and potentially for fertiliser demand.
viewpoints.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

viewpoints.title: Overall fertiliser usage in Ireland expected to remain stable in 2025/26
viewpoints.description: Teagasc predicts that the overall level of fertiliser use in Ireland for the 2025/26 fertiliser year (ending September 2026) will remain in line with the previous year. This stability in volume occurs despite significant price increases. While nitrogen fertiliser sales saw a slight increase in the first half, caution from grassland farmers and reduced tillage area may temper overall consumption, leading to a neutral outlook for total volume.
viewpoints.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

viewpoints.title: Middle East conflict to compress agricultural margins via higher fertiliser costs
viewpoints.description: Bank of Ireland indicates that the Middle East conflict will materially impact agricultural margins in Ireland, primarily through inflated input costs such as fertilisers and fuel. Rising prices, particularly for nitrogen fertiliser due to natural gas price hikes, are outstripping output prices. This margin compression for farmers could lead to reduced demand or changes in purchasing patterns for fertilisers, posing a cautious outlook for the fertiliser industry's sales volumes and profitability.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Ireland less exposed to immediate fertiliser supply issues in 2026
viewpoints.description: Bank of Ireland notes that Ireland is less exposed to immediate fertiliser supply challenges in 2026 compared to other regions. This short-term resilience is attributed to the fact that the majority of fertiliser for the current season was already on farms or within the supply chain before the full impact of recent geopolitical disruptions materialized. This provides a temporary buffer against global market volatility, offering a cautious positive outlook for short-term supply stability.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

pnl_drivers.description: International fertiliser prices reflect production costs heavily related to energy prices, particularly natural gas feedstock for nitrogenous fertilisers. Natural gas price rises translate to higher fertiliser production costs which are then passed on as higher selling prices.

market_sizing.methodology: Fertiliser prices in Ireland are projected to be approximately 20% higher in 2026 compared to 2025 levels. This increase is driven by the rise in energy prices, particularly European natural gas, which directly impacts production costs for fertilisers. The forecast reflects prevailing market conditions influenced by geopolitical events.
market_sizing.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

demand_drivers.description: Farmers increased nitrogen fertiliser purchases to pre-empt expected price increases related to geopolitical conflict and supply disruptions, driving a short-term boost in sales volume.

market_sizing.methodology: Nitrogen fertiliser sales volume in Ireland increased by 7% during the first six months of the 2025/26 fertiliser year (October 2025 to March 2026), compared to the same period in the previous year (2024/25). This increase is attributed to short-term attempts by farmers to pre-empt further price increases due to the Strait of Hormuz conflict.
market_sizing.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

pnl_drivers.description: Rising international fertiliser prices, driven by increased energy costs, are directly translating into higher expenditure for farmers, even with stable consumption volumes. This impacts the cost structure for agricultural businesses.

market_sizing.methodology: Overall expenditure on fertiliser in Ireland is forecast to increase by approximately 20% in 2026, primarily reflecting the 20% increase in fertiliser prices. The overall level of fertiliser use in the 2025/26 fertiliser year is forecast to remain in line with the previous fertiliser year, meaning the increase in expenditure is solely price-driven rather than volume-driven.
market_sizing.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026
